title: Inaction in action
hookLine: the busiest person in the Gita says his work never touches him, and explains how
carry: inaction in action: work without clutching the fruit

cards: A nurse on a double shift. A grandmother cooking for twenty. Everything is happening around them, and somehow nothing seems to be happening to them.

They're working hard, but they aren't grabbing. Then there's the person who does one small task and carries it around all day: did they like it, will it work, what will people say? Same work, completely different weight.
Krishna has just said he comes into the world again and again. Now he says something stranger: all that coming and acting never binds him. And he tells Arjuna how the same can be true of a person.

teach.b: Chapter four, verses nine to twenty-three. Krishna begins with himself. Actions don't stain me, he says, because I have no craving for their fruit, and whoever understands that isn't bound by action either.
Then he admits this is hard. What is action, and what is inaction?
So he gives a riddle, verse eighteen: the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people. Read it slowly.

Some people sit perfectly still and are churning inside, grabbing at outcomes all day long. That's action hiding in inaction. Others move fast, doing a hundred things, and inside they're quiet, not clutching.
That's inaction in action. The body can be busy while the grip is loose. The next verses describe that person.
They give up clinging to the fruit. They're content, depending on nothing. Even fully engaged in work, the text says, they do nothing at all, in the sense that matters.
They take what comes, and stay even in success and in failure.
And verse twenty-three says their work melts away, without the sticky residue karma usually leaves. Notice what Krishna doesn't say: stop working.
Arjuna wanted to walk off the field, and the answer keeps coming back: act. Just act without the hook in you.

teach.h: THE WORK IS REAL. THE CHAIN IS OPTIONAL.
teach.b: The work is real. The chain is optional. Hindus call this way karma yoga, the yoga of action.

how: Some Hindus treat Gita 4.18 as a daily discipline: they work fully, try not to cling to the outcome, and often dedicate a task to God before starting it.

o: the karma of a wrong deed

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna tells Arjuna to stop working to stay free
he keeps saying act. the freedom is in letting go of the fruit, not the work.
the Gita admits even the wise are confused about action
verse 16: what is action, what is inaction? even the wise are bewildered.
sitting still always counts as inaction
verse 18: someone still on the outside can be full of action inside.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you've heard that action binds. what does Krishna say the wise person does?
o: acts fully, without clinging to the fruit.
acts only when the outcome is certain.
games.why: they act, and let the grip go. verse 20: even fully engaged in work, they do nothing at all, in the sense that binds.

practice: Think of one task waiting for you, and picture yourself doing it fully, hands and attention on it.
Notice what comes along with it, the worry about how it'll turn out or who will see it, and on each out-breath loosen your grip on that part: keep the task, set down the grabbing.
If you pray, you can offer the task to Krishna before you begin it.

wordCard.voice: Akarma. Inaction: seeing it inside action is wise. Doing the work fully, without clutching at its fruit, so the work doesn't bind you.

orig.note: Sanskrit: akarma, inaction. a (not) + karma (action). verse 18 asks you to see it inside action.

carryVoice: Your line: inaction in action, work without clutching the fruit. Your hand on the work, not on the result. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.16–4.18 (action, inaction, and the riddle)
